newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE HOPES TO NEAR EMU GOAL IN 97 AUSTERE BUDGET.
newsitem.headline: GREECE HOPES TO NEAR EMU GOAL IN 97 AUSTERE BUDGET.

text.p: Greece's socialist government is expected to unveil details of a tight 1997 budget on Tuesday in hopes it will pave the way for EMU participation at the end of this decade or in the first two years of the 21th century.
The cabinet is going to convene on Tuesday morning to discuss the 1997 budget and Premier Costas Simitis is expected to speak to reporters afterwards.
And National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou will hold a press conference on the budget after the meeting in the afternoon.
The official presentation of the 1997 budget will take place in late November, national economy and finance ministry officials told Reuters.

Simitis who won a fresh four-year mandate on September 22 is widely expected to stress Greece's commitment to European Monetary Union by sticking to a convergence plan to align its economy with the rest of the European Union.

"The cost of non-participation in the European Monetary Union in huge," Simitis told the socialist party's central committee and parliamentary group on Monday. "We can change Greece's image.. The future is defined by us today."

National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou is likely to announce that the 1997 general government budget deficit will fall to 4.2 percent of GDP in line with the EU convergence plan from an expected 7.6 percent of GDP in 1996.
The budget deficit is scheduled to drop under the three percent of GDP Maastricht threshold, seen at 2.4 percent of GDP in 1998.

The Greek general government budget deficit has been on a downward projectory in the last few years dropping to 9.2 percent of GDP in 1995 from 13.1 percent in 1994 on the heels of smaller central government budget deficits and surpluses recorded by public entities.
According to the latest press leaks, the fiscal consolidation in 1997 will be based on boosting tax and non-tax revenues and applying a much needed freeze in real spending.

The budget deficit reduction in 1997 will come from savings of one trillion drachmas or more which will be the result of a high revenue growth rate of about 15 percent or more and an increase in nominal expenditures between six and seven percent.

The bulk of revenues is expected to come from increased direct taxes as many tax breaks will be abolished leading to a rise in taxable incomes, the non-indexation of the income tax scale for the fifth straight year and a host of new taxes on real estate, interest on state securities and financial products.

A withholding tax of 7.5 percent is to be applied to interest earned on new government securities effective early December or January 1997 and a 15 percent tax will be levied on financial products including derivitatives.

Mutual funds will face a new tax of two to five per thousand on their assets under management but it is still unclear whether the current 15 percent withholding tax on income from state securities and repos will be maintained.
Commercial banks are also likely to see their corporate marginal tax rate go up to 40 percent from 35 percent to provide much needed funds for the revenue hungry budget.

A pick up in indirect taxes will also be planned based on a stronger GDP growth likely to be set at 3.3 percent in 1997 from an expected 2.6 percent in 1996. It will be coupled by yet another crack down on tax evasion.

Spending is likely to be projected to rise about six percent, about the same as projected average inflation. The wage bill will likely rise by about 8.5 percent and interest payments on public debt by much less.
Yet capital expenditures are expected to soar to about 30 percent to make sure that Greece absorbs all of its European Union funds in an effort to fuel economic growth.
The government has already submitted a draft bill to parliament comprised of 14 measures to control spending and do away with some public sector waste.

New hirings with the exception of teachers will be limited to 20 percent of retirements, subsidies to public utilities will be curtailed and many off-budget items that have been partly blamed for a high debt to GDP ratio will be included in the budget.
Greece's debt to GDP ratio has failed to record a noticeable improvement despite falling interest rates on public debt and larger primary surpluses as a percent of GDP.
"Below the line" items such as the issuance of restructuring bonds for state banks and public organisations are mainly responsible for a stubborn debt-to-GDP ratio. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
